findings.title: Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context
findings.body: Create derives the legacy-write context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the incoming request context, and Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection do the same. That parent is cancelled when the HTTP handler finishes, normally shortly after the unified-storage response is encoded, so the nominal 10-second timeout rarely applies. Legacy writes therefore race response completion and are frequently aborted after the client has received success, silently leaving unified storage and legacy storage diverged. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving required values before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy Create races the caller on the same mutable object
findings.body: Create passes obj to Storage.Create and then captures the same obj in a background goroutine while returning created to the API server. Storage implementations commonly mutate and return the passed object, so created may alias obj. The API server can encode or further mutate the returned object while Legacy.Create concurrently reads or mutates it, causing a data race and potentially changing the response or the object persisted to legacy storage. A deep copy must be made for the legacy write before returning, rather than sharing the request object with the goroutine.

findings.title: Legacy Update re-runs UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the unified-storage result
findings.body: Update passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. The legacy store will invoke UpdatedObject a second time against its own old object, so fields derived from the old object, defaults, resource version, or other update logic can produce an object different from res, the object actually written to unified storage. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to give legacy storage exactly the unified-storage result; removing that wrapper reintroduces a consistency risk between the two stores.

findings.title: A unified-storage Delete error abandons the legacy delete
findings.body: Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy storage, for example because it predates migration, a backfill missed it, or an earlier asynchronous create/update failed, will therefore never be deleted from legacy storage. The client receives an error based on unified storage while the legacy orphan remains and can reappear if the resource is later returned to a legacy-reading mode. The previous behavior still attempted the legacy delete when unified storage reported NotFound.

findings.title: Mode 3 duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label
findings.body: Several metric calls are misattributed: a Storage.Create failure at line 45 records recordLegacyDuration, a Storage.Update failure at line 129 also records recordLegacyDuration, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 records recordStorageDuration, and successful Delete at line 106 passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts legacy-versus-storage latency and error measurements and, for Delete, creates a high-cardinality kind label containing user object names.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The Mode 3 Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection tests assert only the synchronous unified-storage result and return without waiting for or asserting completion of the background legacy goroutine. They would pass if the legacy write were removed or always failed, and the unsynchronized goroutine can still access the shared mock and shared example objects after the test has finished, creating flaky behavior under the race detector. The tests need a synchronization mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was called with the expected arguments.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist integration tests assume synchronous legacy visibility
findings.body: The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately checks the legacy playlist APIs after Kubernetes create and update operations through helpers such as the legacy search check and getFromBothAPIs. Mode 3 performs legacy writes asynchronously with no completion signal, so those assertions race the background legacy write and can intermittently observe missing or stale legacy playlists even when the implementation eventually succeeds. The mode 3 scenarios need eventual-consistency polling for legacy assertions or a different set of expectations from the synchronous modes.
